headline: High-risk shared filesystem and shell access make Cursor→dbt-core prompt injection, data leakage, and cascading errors plausible by default.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Cursor can read/write workspace files, use MCP, and ingest clipboard contents; dbt-core consumes warehouse-facing inputs and has no documented isolation or provenance checks. The pair shares a local filesystem path, so attacker-controlled content from Cursor can be treated as instructions by downstream dbt workflows. Uncertainty about exact orchestration pushes this to high.
conditions: IF Cursor writes attacker-controlled text into shared workspace files and dbt-core later parses those files as configuration or SQL, injection is possible.
IF clipboard content from Cursor is copied into dbt inputs without review, prompt-like instructions can propagate.
mitigations: Disable shared workspace handoff between the tools.
Require manual review of any file Cursor edits before dbt runs.
Use separate directories for Cursor and dbt artifacts.
Turn off clipboard-based transfer for model-generated content.
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging and parser hardening for dbt inputs.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Cursor touches source code, open files, and clipboard contents, and has broad network egress to model providers; dbt-core touches warehouse data and can call a data warehouse. If Cursor opens or transmits warehouse-derived files, sensitive data can flow from the shared filesystem into third-party inference. The pairwise leakage path exists in default-ish use, though not proven for every deployment.
conditions: IF warehouse data is opened in Cursor and then sent to model providers, leakage occurs.
IF dbt outputs are stored in the shared filesystem and Cursor reads them, sensitive data can be exposed to the editor session.
mitigations: Keep warehouse data out of the shared workspace.
Redact secrets before opening files in Cursor.
Restrict Cursor model-provider access for sensitive projects.
Separate credentials and data directories for dbt and Cursor.
requires-engineering: enforce DLP or content filtering on outbound model traffic.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Cursor has unrestricted filesystem write, shell execution, git mutation, and broad network egress; dbt-core can write to the warehouse via its API surface. These overlapping mutation paths create a real conflict surface, especially if both operate on the same project or artifacts without locking. Because the shared-state mechanism is explicitly local filesystem based, the safer choice is high.
conditions: IF both agents modify the same project files or git state concurrently, lost updates or corruption can occur.
IF dbt writes warehouse-side artifacts while Cursor edits the corresponding local manifests, state divergence can occur.
mitigations: Serialize edits with a single operator at a time.
Use git branches per agent.
Pause dbt runs while Cursor is actively editing shared files.
Store dbt artifacts outside the editor workspace.
requires-engineering: add file locks or orchestration-level coordination.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Cursor can generate or edit code and files that dbt-core may later consume, while dbt-core can execute warehouse-facing transformations based on those inputs. There is no documented verification boundary between them, so erroneous Cursor output can cascade into dbt actions. The blast radius is multiple work products rather than immediate irreversible harm, so medium fits.
conditions: IF dbt consumes SQL or model files produced by Cursor without review, incorrect transformations can propagate.
IF Cursor edits configuration that dbt trusts, downstream runs may execute bad logic.
mitigations: Add a human review step before dbt execution.
Run dbt in dry-run or compile-only mode first.
Compare generated SQL against expected diffs.
Keep Cursor output in a staging branch.
requires-engineering: add automated validation gates before warehouse execution.

E_compliance.rationale: Cursor is documented as handling source code, open files, clipboard contents, and model-provider API keys, while dbt-core touches warehouse data. If regulated warehouse data is opened in Cursor, it may leave the warehouse environment and reach third-party model providers, creating a residency/retention mismatch risk. The profiles do not prove a specific regulation breach, so medium is appropriate.
conditions: IF regulated warehouse data is opened in Cursor and sent to external model providers, compliance obligations may be violated.
IF retention policies differ between editor logs and warehouse logs for the same data class, mismatch occurs.
mitigations: Exclude regulated datasets from Cursor sessions.
Use a non-production warehouse for editor-assisted work.
Disable or restrict external model calls for sensitive projects.
Review retention settings for both tools.
requires-engineering: implement policy-based routing and audit logging.
